issue.title: statistics-graph card ignores the days_to_show parameter

repository.name: core
repository.description: :house_with_garden: Open source home automation that puts local control and privacy first.

issue.body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have updated to the latest available Home Assistant version.
- [X] I have cleared the cache of my browser.
- [X] I have tried a different browser to see if it is related to my browser.

### Describe the issue you are experiencing

The time horizon displayed got independent from the `days_to_show` parameter.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5061219/171565892-b7649432-b62c-49b4-add1-795fc6d07bd0.png)


### Describe the behavior you expected

Display only the specified time, as it worked previously.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

Set `days_to_show ` to any value, it is ignored.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

2022.6.0

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

2022.5.x

### In which browser are you experiencing the issue with?

any (IE, FF, Chrome Win and Android)

### Which operating system are you using to run this browser?

Android 8.0.0, Win 7

### State of relevant entities

_No response_

### Problem-relevant frontend configuration

```yaml
type: vertical-stack
cards:
  - type: statistics-graph
    title: 30 days
    chart_type: line
    period: hour
    days_to_show: 30
    entities:
      - entity: sensor.living_room_temperature_average_for_heater
        name: Temperature
      - entity: sensor.living_room_humidity_average_for_dehumidifier
        name: Humidity
      - entity: sensor.terrace_temperature_average
        name: Temperature›
      - entity: sensor.terrace_humidity_average
        name: Humidity›
    stat_types:
      - mean
  - type: statistics-graph
    title: 180 days
    chart_type: line
    period: day
    days_to_show: 180
    entities:
      - entity: sensor.living_room_temperature_average_for_heater
        name: °C
      - entity: sensor.living_room_humidity_average_for_dehumidifier
        name: '%'
      - entity: sensor.terrace_temperature_average
        name: °C›
      - entity: sensor.terrace_humidity_average
        name: '%›'
    stat_types:
      - min
      - max
      - mean
```


### Javascript errors shown in your browser console/inspector

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_

body:
> well the error is clear, and part of what lambda stmt does is that it does hold a single copy of a "statement" around. There are then some "memoized" attributes on objects like Select that are evaluated just once, such as during string compilation, so those together make this condition plausible.
> 
> We would observe, if you can confirm, that the error occurs only once and very early in the application's runtime; once the Select object has all of its memoized elements initialized, there should be no further modifications to dict.

I agree. The users who have the issue reported that if the problem happens, it happens for the life of the run, and their data is wrong. If they restart, everything works out, and sometimes we hit the failure mode. The most common case is where they have both humidity and temp sensors, and they happen to generate history simultaneously, and the data gets swapped. I've not been able to replicate the issue in my testing, but I suspect that it's because my hardware is too fast, so there is far less chance of the two threads being at the same place at the same time. Based on the home assistant issue queue, the problem is far easier to repro on raspberry pi 2 and 3, so the slower the hardware, the more likely this is to happen since there is more time that both threads could be hitting the same place.  
Adding some prints into `sql.visitors.replacement_traverse` was enough to slow things down enough that I started to see unexpected behavior from what I think is the bindparms being swapped and the result is getting unexpected data. Still, I could never get it to raise the RuntimeError.
> 
> Also, as we see in my POC below, at least on my end this error does not seem to occur in Python 3.10, but does occur in Python 3.8 and 3.9. So this would suggest an upgrade to Python 3.10 would resolve immediately.

Thanks.  Home Assistant will drop python 3.9 support in [January 2023](https://github.com/home-assistant/architecture/blob/master/adr/0002-minimum-supported-python-version.md), but that's what the bulk of the install base is using so sadly that won't be a quick fix.

> 
> Proposal is to apply list() to this particular clone method, which as an implementation detail would appear to cause the iteration to proceed atomically even though the items() method that returns an iterable ItemsView is still returned. The below case includes two functions "one()" and "one_proposed_protected()", if you want to play w/ this case so that we can agree on an approach.
> 
> ```python
> import threading
> ```

That seems like a good solution to me, and I confirmed Running this with 3.9.12 with the thread target changed to `one_proposed_protected` does not generate any `RuntimeError`

Running this with 3.9.12 as-is
```
dictionary changed size during iteration
dictionary changed size during iteration
dictionary keys changed during iteration
dictionary changed size during iteration
```

Once you have a proposed commit, we can ask @lmagyar to test as he has been able to make this happen almost on demand

Thanks Mike!

body: oh also that "skip" list is usually empty, so we normally can use copy() here, there's another clone routine like this one which does that, so will make them  both the same and use list(dict.items()) if skip is non-empty

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**use copy(), list(items()) for clone / generate operations** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3901

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_1_4** branch:

**use copy(), list(items()) for clone / generate operations** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3902

I added back the debug prints to slow things down and it seems like the inconsistency is gone, but its hard to tell if I'm just lucky or its a good fix as this is not a good test.  I've asked the user who could repo this reliably to test here https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/72991#issuecomment-1149069171

```diff
diff -ru sqlalchemy/sql/visitors.py /Users/bdraco/sqlalchemy_debug/sql/visitors.py
--- sqlalchemy/sql/visitors.py  2022-06-06 21:45:55.000000000 -1000
+++ /Users/bdraco/sqlalchemy_debug/sql/visitors.py      2022-06-06 21:23:57.000000000 -1000
@@ -810,6 +810,8 @@
     as is a common use case within the ORM.

     """
+    import pprint
+    pprint.pprint(['replacement_traverse',obj,opts,replace])

     cloned = {}
     stop_on = {id(x) for x in opts.get("stop_on", [])}
@@ -834,6 +836,8 @@
                 # vice versa
                 id_elem = id(elem)
                 if id_elem not in cloned:
+                    import pprint
+                    pprint.pprint(['elmn', elem, 'newelem',newelem,'id_elem',id_elem])
                     if "replace" in kw:
                         newelem = kw["replace"](elem)
                         if newelem is not None:
```

Based on the feedback here https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/72991#issuecomment-1149111962 it looks like there is still another race that hasn't been uncovered or there is more going on here.
I'm going to work some more on trying to get a smaller reproducer today now that we have a better idea where in the code the issue lies

body:
so they are not getting the dictionary size error, but the lambda is still wrong, is that it?  because the lambda being wrong didn't seem right

I would suggest not using the lambda as performance shouldn't be much worse using a regular cached statement.  the lambda thing is really close to being useful but ultimately it's just too spooky.

> so they are not getting the dictionary size error, but the lambda is still wrong, is that it? because the lambda being wrong didn't seem right

That seems to be the case. It seems like only the bindparams are affected.  I've been digging though 
https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/e347aa81a593252b6ee4f84a411f62f526ba0c77/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/lambdas.py#L327 to see if I can find the issue but no luck yet.
> 
> I would suggest not using the lambda as performance shouldn't be much worse using a regular cached statement. the lambda thing is really close to being useful but ultimately it's just too spooky.

We replaced ~50 baked queries with the lambdas since baked is going away?  The lambdas seem to be much faster replacing the bindparams the last time I looked.  It would be nice if we can figure this out since rewriting all those to remove the lambdas is no small task.

## Proposed change
<!--
  Describe the big picture of your changes here to communicate to the
  maintainers why we should accept this pull request. If it fixes a bug
  or resolves a feature request, be sure to link to that issue in the
  additional information section.
-->
It looks like these need a bit more time to mature upstream per
https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/8098#issuecomment-1149157104
so let's rip them out any place where we need to worry
about thread safety.

There will likely be another sqlalchemy bump for
https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/8098 in the future
as that problem seems to be more generic. Its likely that problem will
present as a raised exception failure state. All evidence suggests that
the lambdas have another undiscovered different thread safety 
issue since the proposed fix there didn't solve the inconsistencies with the lambdas.

I left them in purge and the recorder thread because the problems
are thread safety issues and these queries are always single threaded
and I didn't want to risk causing a regression of #71015

While this will make the queries slower, slower and correct
is better than fast and incorrect.

Likely fixes #65499

body:
We are going to drop the lambda in places where the queries are multi-threaded.  So its not so big of a change as I expected.

I assume this problem can happen outside of lambdas as well but its far less likely?

> 
> We replaced ~50 baked queries with the lambdas since baked is going away? The lambdas seem to be much faster replacing the bindparams the last time I looked. It would be nice if we can figure this out since rewriting all those to remove the lambdas is no small task.

so yes the lambdas are definitely extremely fast, however, in 1.4 all statements that show up in the logs as "Generated / cached" are cached regardless, which should be the vast majority of DQL and DML statements.  lambdas just make the caching even faster.   compared to baked queries, lambdas are probably the same speed and the default caching will be a little less fast depending on the complexity of the query, since it's the "building up the query" and "generating the cache key" part that is still relatively resource intensive (though not nearly as much as the Core / ORM compilation which is the vast majority of query rendering, which is all cached now).     We hope to convert more and more of the remaining process to use cython in the 2.0 series.

so from that, as far as lambdas making mistakes, if you were able to get a reproducer case I could probably fix the issue, however, one reason I've backed way off of lambdas is that the reproducers are extremely difficult to come up with, we've already had a bunch of these very scary lambda caching bugs in the early 1.4 releases which is what led me to take it out of the ORM's internals, was not really worth it.

But I would certainly love to fix the issue if we could narrow down what it is.   if it's even that we have to put a mutex when the lambda first generates its internal state, that's fine, just would need to know what scope it needs to be and if that is actually the problem.

> We are going to drop the lambda in places where the queries are multi-threaded. 

so towards that mutexing issue, if you were able to reproduce, seeing if mutexes on those functions resolved it would help to narrow down if that's something we could do on our end.

> I assume this problem can happen outside of lambdas as well but its far less likely?

if you're just making new select() etc. objects on the fly that aren't shared among threads I think there is no risk at all for this kind of issue, the regular caching has been in use across millions of downloads for about a year and we haven't had any issues since the first early releases.  it's much simpler in its implementation than the lambda thing is.

I will work some more on coming up with a reproducer once we have this all ironed out and I have a bit more uninterrupted time to work on this. 👍

Thankfully many of Home Assistant's performance sensitive ones with the large cache keys are all running in a single thread so the impact of removing be lambdas isn't as bad as I had initially feared.
so...I should probably commit this fix, right?  did it at least eliminate the "dictionary size changed" issue?
